title: Why do we randomize?
text:
Introduction
In our previous post, Introduction to A/B Testing, we discussed how A/B testing can be used to assess whether a given modification causes a change in a variable of interest. For example, whether increasing the size of the shopping cart icon increases sales.
We also said that A/B testing involves splitting website traffic into the current version (A or control) and the modified version (B or treatment), and that this split needs to be random. But why?


Confounding factors
To understand the importance of randomization, we need to talk briefly about confounding factors.
Suppose we want to evaluate whether a medication improves survival from COVID-19. However, other variables can affect survival. For instance, younger people are more likely to survive than older people. If we give the medication only to younger people and withhold it from older people, the treated group may appear to have higher survival, not because the medication works, but because it contains younger patients who are intrinsically more likely to survive.
Similarly, clinicians might be tempted to give the medication only to high-risk patients. High-risk patients are, by definition, more likely to die. In that case, if we compare the treated group with the untreated group, the treated group might show lower survival, that could lead to a mistaken conclusion that the medication is ineffective. The poorer outcome could simply reflect the greater baseline risk in the treated group.
These scenarios illustrate confounding variables, which variables that can affect both the treatment (the modification) and the observed outcome (survival). This is represented in Figure 1.






Figure 1: Confounding: a third variable influences both treatment assignment and outcome.



This is one of the reasons by we need to randomize, because similar profile of subjects would go to the treatment and control groups, that would eliminate what is so called selection bias


Ceteris Paribus
Ceteris Paribus: “All other things being equal”
Ceteris Paribus is a latin word that describes the situation between two groups that have all of the characterincts being the same, except for your provided modifcation. In our COVID medication, a Ceteris Paribus situation would make the treatment and control groups having the same characteriscts (similar age profile, similar sex profile, etc), except for the medication which is being provided in the treatment group.
What technique provide this Ceteris Paribus scenario: RANDOMIZATION.

title: Average Treatment Effect
text:
Recap
In previous posts, Introduction to A/B Testing and Importance of Randomization, we introduced A/B testing and why randomization is such an important step. Now we want to discuss how we can measure the effect of our proposed modification (the treatment).


Average Treatment Effect (ATE)
The Average Treatment Effect (ATE) measures the expected effect of a proposed treatment. In our COVID-19 example from Importance of Randomization, where we assess whether a medication improves survival. The ATE, in this case, would be the increase in the survival rate.
Consider a subject i with two potential outcomes: Y_i^{(1)} if treated and Y_i^{(0)} if not treated. The individual treatment effect is: 
Y_i^{(1)} - Y_i^{(0)}
 If subject i actually received the treatment, we do not observe Y_i^{(0)}. This unobserved outcome is the counterfactual.
The population Average Treatment Effect (ATE) is: 
\mathrm{ATE} = \mathbb{E}\!\left[Y^{(1)} - Y^{(0)}\right] = \sum _j^N (Y_j^{(1)} - Y_j^{(0)})

Because the counterfactual for each individual is unobserved, we estimate the ATE by comparing randomized groups. If we randomize N subjects to treatment and N to control, a consistent estimator is:

\widehat{\mathrm{ATE}} = \overline{Y}^{(1)} - \overline{Y}^{(0)}
 the difference in average outcomes between the treated and control groups. With sufficiently large N, randomization makes the groups comparable, allowing us to estimate the ATE without observing individual counterfactuals.

title: Sampling
text:
Whenever you try to learn something about a real population, a practical limitation appears. It is almost never possible to measure every individual. The cost is high and time is limited. This is why sampling is so important.






Figure 1: Getting a sample from a population.

title: Sampling
text:
Random variables
A random variable is a mathematical representation of a process that produces uncertain outcomes.
For example, the height of a person selected at random from a country can be represented by a random variable (X). The population has a true mean height (\mu) and a true standard deviation (\sigma). These values describe the distribution of (X).
Once we actually measure the height of a selected person, we obtain a concrete value. This observed value is called a realization. If our first sampled height is 171 cm, then (x_1 = 171). This means that 171 is the realization of the random variable (X_1).
Before measurement, (X_1) is random. After measurement, (x_1 = 171) is fixed.
OBS: We use capital letters for random variables and lowercase letters for their realizations.

title: Sampling
text:
Expectation
The expectation of a random variable is its theoretical long run average. If we could repeat the random process infinitely many times, the average of all generated values would approach the expectation.
For the height variable (X):

E[X] = \mu

The expectation is a theoretical value defined by the population. The sample average is computed from a finite set of observed data. If the sample size grows without bound, the sample average converges to the expectation. For a finite sample, they are generally different.

title: Sampling
text:
The sample mean
The observed sample mean is defined as:

\bar{x} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N x_i

Before observing the data, the sample mean itself is a random variable:

\bar{X} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N X_i

This explains why different samples produce different sample means. The randomness comes from the (X_i).

title: Sampling
text:
Expectation of the sample mean
Each sample will produce a different sample mean. What would be the long run average of these sample means? In other words, what is the expected value of the random variable (\bar{X})?

E[\bar{X}] = E\left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N X_i\right)
= \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N E[X_i]

Since each (X_i) has mean (\mu):

E[\bar{X}] = \mu

The expectation of the sample mean equals the true mean of the population. This does not imply that any observed (\bar{x}) equals (\mu). It only guarantees that the estimator is correct on average in the long run.

title: Sampling
text:
Variance of the sample mean
Assuming the sampled values are independent:

Var(\bar{X}) = Var\left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N X_i\right)
= \frac{\sigma^2}{N}

The variability of the sample mean decreases as the sample size increases. Larger samples produce more stable estimates.

title: Sampling
text:
The Central Limit Theorem
Even if the population distribution is not normal, the Central Limit Theorem states that for sufficiently large (N):

\bar{X} \sim N\left(\mu, \frac{\sigma^2}{N}\right)

title: Sampling
text:
How to estimate (\mu) and (\sigma)?
In real applications, we usually have only one sample of size (N). Since the population parameters (\mu) and (\sigma) are unknown, we replace them with estimates from the data:

\mu \approx \bar{x}

and

\sigma \approx s

Where (s) is the sample standard deviation.
Using these estimates, we approximate the distribution of the sample mean for large (N) by:

\bar{X} \sim N\left(\bar{x}, \frac{s^2}{N}\right)

title: Introduction to A/B testing
text:
Introduction
Suppose you run an online store and want to improve sales. You then have an idea to enlarge the shopping-cart button. After deploying the change, sales increase (see Figure 1).






Figure 1: Sales trend after introducing the cart-size change.



Did your modification cause the increase in sales?
Not necessarily. Several other factors could explain the rise, such as seasonality. For instance, if you implemented the change in early December, sales might climb simply because it’s close to Christmas, when people usually buy more.
To argue that your modification caused the increase, we first need a clear notion of causality.


What is causality?
Correlation is about variables moving together. Causality is about changing in one variable producing changes in another.
In broad terms, two variables (A) and (B) are correlated when changes in one tend to be associated with changes in the other (see Figure 2). Correlation alone does not establish a cause–effect relationship.






Figure 2: An illustration of variables moving together (correlation).



Two things can be correlated without either causing the other. This is called spurious correlation.
A classic spurious correlation example is shown in Figure 3:
(A=) “Air quality in Union City, Tennessee” and (B=) “Number of movies featuring Orlando Bloom.” They are correlated, but there is no plausible causal link between them.






Figure 3: A spurious correlation example: unrelated variables that co-vary.



Causality, on the other hand, concerns cause and consequence: if we change (A), what happens to (B)?
Consider Figure 4. An oven’s temperature (B) is controlled by a dial (A). A thermometer (C) responds to the temperature. Turning the dial (A) changes the temperature (B), and the temperature (B) moves the thermometer (C). Thus, (A B C). Here, (A) and (C) are correlated because of the causal chain, but (A) does not act directly on (C). The effect is mediated by (B).






Figure 4: Correlation via a causal chain (mediation).



With this foundation, we can now discuss A/B testing.


What is A/B testing?
A/B testing is a practical way to evaluate causality. It helps answer questions like: Did increasing the cart size cause higher sales?
In an A/B test you create two variants of the same experience. In our website example:

A (control): the current website.
B (treatment): the website with your proposed change.

See Figure 5.






Figure 5: A/B test with a control (A) and a treatment (B).



To assess whether the modification improves sales, you randomly split incoming traffic between A and B. Because assignment is random, the two groups tend to be similar on both observed and unobserved factors. Any persistent difference in outcomes (e.g., conversion rate, revenue per session) is then can be attributable to the modification itself.
In short, A/B testing provides a clean comparison between “before/without change” (A) and “with change” (B) under randomization, offering strong evidence about whether your change causes an improvement.
A/B tests are the only model-free way to show causality.

title: Einsum Tutorial
text:
Einstein summation notation, commonly denoted as einsum, is a powerful tool for performing optimized matrix operations. It allows us to avoid using unnecessary for loops and simplifies complex matrix manipulations, making code more readable and efficient.
Einsum is available in different libraries such as Numpy, PyTorch and Tensorflow.

title: Einsum Tutorial
Einsum Tutorial
text:
Intuition
The einsum operation performs two fundamental actions over tensors: multiplication and summation.
We now explore the logic behind both.

Multiplication
Let A and B be two 3 \times 3 matrices. We create another matrix C whose elements are obtained from elementwise multiplication:

c_{ij} = a_{ij} b_{ij}

Python:
import numpy as np
A = np.random.random((3, 3))
B = np.random.random((3, 3))
C = np.multiply(A, B)
Using einsum:
C = np.einsum("ij,ij->ij", A, B)
This mirrors the mathematical expression c_{ij} = a_{ij} b_{ij}.
We can also express it as a loop:
C = np.zeros((3, 3))
for i in range(3):
    for j in range(3):
        C[i, j] = A[i, j] * B[i, j]
Let us now work with vectors. For v = [1, 2, 3] and p = [4, 5, 6]:

z_i = v_i p_i

Using einsum:
z = np.einsum("i,i->i", v, p)
Using loops:
z = np.zeros(3)
for i in range(3):
    z[i] = v[i] * p[i]
Now consider using different indices, "i,j":
np.einsum("i,j->ij", v, p)
This produces all combinations v_i p_j and forms a 3 \times 3 matrix. Loop equivalent:
for i in range(3):
    for j in range(3):
        C[i, j] = v[i] * p[j]


Summation
einsum also performs summation over indices. If an index appears in the input but not in the output, the summation is applied over that index.
To sum all elements of a vector a:
Math notation:

c = \sum_i a_i

Einsum:
c = np.einsum("i->", a)
To sum all elements of a matrix A:
s = np.einsum("ij->", A)


Matrix multiplication
Let A be a 2 \times 3 matrix and B a 3 \times 2 matrix. Their product C = AB has components:

c_{ik} = \sum_j a_{ij} b_{jk}

Einsum:
C = np.einsum("ij,jk->ik", A, B)

title: Einsum Tutorial
text:
Practice

1. Transpose a matrix
The transpose of A = [a_{ij}] is A^{\mathsf{T}} = [a_{ji}].
Using einsum:
C = np.einsum("ij->ji", A)


2. Compute the trace of a square matrix
For a square matrix:

A = \begin{bmatrix}
a_{11} & a_{12} \\
a_{21} & a_{22}
\end{bmatrix}

The trace is:

\operatorname{Tr}(A) = \sum_i a_{ii}

Using einsum:
tr = np.einsum("ii->", A)


3. Compute the Euclidean norm of a vector

\|v\| = \sqrt{\sum_i v_i v_i}

Using einsum:
norm = np.sqrt(np.einsum("i,i->", v, v))


4. Batch matrix multiplication
Let A be a batch of matrices with shape (n, p, h) and B be a batch of matrices with shape (n, h, u).
The batch product is:

c_{nik} = \sum_j a_{nij} b_{njk}

Using einsum:
C = np.einsum("nij,njk->nik", A, B)

title: Hypothesis-driven Product Development
text:
In our previous posts, we introduced A/B testing, highlighted why randomization is essential, and discussed how we can measure the effect of a treatment in an A/B testing context.
Today we move into Hypothesis-driven Product Development (HDPD), which shifts the traditional product workflow from simply having an idea, implementing it, and checking results to a structured process where ideas are tested through experimentation and validated with measurable evidence.

title: Hypothesis-driven Product Development
text:
Good metrics
A metric is good when it can be compared across time and, for business contexts, when it is connected to financial performance or user behavior. Examples:

CTR (Click Through Rate)
CVR (Conversion Rate)

These metrics help guide decisions because changes in them reflect real impact on the business.
In general, in a given experiment, you have three sorts of metrics:

OEC (Overall evaluation criteria): The most important metric
Secondary metrics: Important metrics, but they are not the OEC
Guardrail metrics: “Security” metrics, metrics that should not be comprimised by the experiment, such as loading time

title: Hypothesis-driven Product Development
text:
Vanity metrics
Metrics are usually created to support meaningful decisions. However, some metrics look impressive but do not help with practical decision making. These are known as “vanity metrics”.
For example, the total number of users who have ever created an account may be useful for marketing announcements, such as saying a product reached one million users, but it does not help you decide how to improve the product.
